what_it_does: When an AI model must produce structured output—like valid JSON or SQL—every word it generates has to be checked against a grammar rulebook, and that checking is slow enough to dominate total runtime. XGrammar makes the check nearly free by recognizing that almost all words in the vocabulary can be pre-approved or pre-rejected once, before any text is generated, leaving only a tiny fraction to be checked on the fly. Integrated with a serving engine, it produces structured output with near-zero added latency.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Constrained decoding works by computing a 'mask' each step: a pass/fail verdict for every word in the model's vocabulary (up to 128,000 words for Llama-3.1), blocking anything that would break the required structure. The naive approach re-runs the full grammar check every step, which is painfully slow.

How it works. XGrammar builds a pushdown automaton—think of it as a stack-based rule machine that tracks how far through the grammar the text has progressed. The key insight is that most vocabulary words only need the top entry of that stack to decide pass or fail; they are 'context-independent.' For Llama-3.1 with JSON grammar, only 1,134 of 128,000 words (less than 1%) are genuinely ambiguous at runtime. XGrammar precomputes verdicts for the rest and stores them in a compact cache keyed by stack position, using only 0.46 MB instead of the 160 MB a naive bitmap would require.

The single key design choice. A 'context expansion' pass further analyzes the grammar to reject most of those remaining 1,134 ambiguous words at precompute time too, shrinking the runtime check list to about 120 words. A persistent execution stack (a shared tree of stack states) lets the system roll back and branch cheaply when the grammar is ambiguous, and lets common word-prefix work be shared across the vocabulary check.

The catch. CPU work for the small residual runtime check is run in parallel with the GPU's attention computation, so it is hidden entirely behind the model's own inference time.

The result. Per-token mask generation drops from tens of milliseconds (competitors) to under 40 microseconds for JSON—up to 100x faster. End-to-end serving with structured output runs as fast as unconstrained serving, with function-calling accuracy rising from 62% to 100%.
